input.question: How is it possible that everything falls at the same speed regardless of mass? Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct?
input.ground_truth: > Is there a limit where this approximation stops to be correct? Yes. The "limit of the approximation" is that the mass of the thing dropped is negligible compared to the mass of the Earth. Consider two masses M1 and M2 at a distance R. The gravitational force F between them will be G\*M1\*M2/R^2 , so the acceleration of the first object will be F/M1 = G\*M2/R^2 and the acceleration of the second object will be F/M2 = G\*M1/R^2 The two objects will thus accelerate towards each other at a rate of G\*(M1 + M2)/R^2 . In the case of a feather or hammer on the Earth, M1 is so much larger than M2 that the effects of M2 can be ignored. In this case, both hammer and feather would have the same acceleration.

Okay! Imagine you drop a feather and a rock at the same time on Earth. You might think the heavy rock will fall faster, right? But if there’s no air (like on the Moon), they both fall down at the same speed! That’s because the air can push on the feather and slow it down, but the rock is too heavy for the air to slow it much.

Now, why do they fall at the same speed (if there’s no air)? Well, there’s something called “gravity” that pulls everything down. But here’s the cool part: gravity pulls harder on things that are heavier, but heavier things are also harder to move! So, it all balances out, and they fall together.

But… there’s a tiny, tiny rule! This “same speed” thing is almost true, but not exactly true if things are super, super fast or super heavy, like planets or rockets. In those cases, we need to use a bigger kid’s math (called “relativity”) to understand what happens. But for things we see every day, like apples or balls, they all fall at the same speed!
